sents.text: Last time you met the terminal.
Today you learn to move around in it: where files live, how to get from one folder to another, and how to make, copy, move and delete things, all without a mouse.
Linux keeps everything in one big tree.
At the very top is the root folder, written as a single forward slash.
Everything else hangs below it: home folders for users, settings in a folder called etc, programs in usr.
In Colab, your work sits in slash content.
A path is the address of a file.
An absolute path starts from the root, with a slash, and works from anywhere.
A relative path starts from where you are now.
If you're already in slash content, then sample data, slash, README dot md points to the same file.
Three shortcuts save a lot of typing.
A single dot means the folder you're in.
Two dots mean the folder one level up.
And the tilde means your home folder.
So cd dot dot moves you up one level, and cd tilde takes you home.
Give it a path, and you're there; check with pwd.
One catch in Colab: every line that starts with an exclamation mark runs in a fresh shell, so a cd there is forgotten on the very next line.
Use percent cd instead, and Colab remembers where you are.
